processing: Sun-dried large-leaf maocha steamed and pressed into 357 g round cakes. The old house is said to have used leaf from Mansong on Yibang mountain.
harvest_season: Not documented for individual antique lots. As with other sheng, spring leaf is the most prized in the modern versions.
appearance_dry: Antique cakes are very dark and aged, identified by the inner ticket: a dragon, horse and pagoda design on the early ones, double lions with a flag on the later ones.
appearance_liquor: Typical of very old sheng, a deep chestnut to red-brown and clear; a modern young cake pours golden as other young sheng do.
appearance_wet: As with other long-aged sheng, soft dark brown leaf.
taste_profile: Few reliable notes exist for the antique cakes. Expect what is typical of very old sheng: woody, earthy and mellow, with little bitterness left.

brewing.notes: General advice for old sheng: a quick rinse and near-boiling water. A modern young cake under the name wants the shorter, gentler handling of any young sheng.

vintage_note: Two different things carry the name. Antique cakes are sold singly at specialist sales and sorted by inner ticket, dragon-and-horse before 1920 and double lion from 1920. The modern company in Jinghong sells new cakes by production year like any other sheng. Do not let a shared name suggest shared age, and treat online antique offers with deep suspicion.
description:
Tongqing Hao is one of the great names of old Yiwu pu-erh, a family tea house whose early round cakes are among the most revered antique teas. The name also survives on a modern company, so check which one you are looking at.

The classic product was a 357 g round cake, and the house is said to have favoured leaf from Mansong on Yibang mountain. Its wrappers and inner tickets are how collectors tell one era from another: first the dragon, white horse and pagoda design, then, after imitators multiplied, a white ticket with blue double lions and a flag.

For taste, honest evidence is thin, since hardly anyone has drunk the old cakes. Very old sheng in general turns soft, woody and earthy. A modern cake bearing the name is a young sheng and should be judged on its own.

Buying means being sceptical. Tea writers specifically warn against hunting for this name on open marketplaces, and an unbelievable price for an antique usually has an obvious explanation. For a modern cake, look for a stated year and raw material.

If the history draws you in, a young Yiwu or Yibang sheng from a trustworthy maker is the affordable way to meet the region.
history:
By the brand's own lineage, the Liu family came from Mayang in Hunan, settled in Shiping in Yunnan with the army in the early Ming, and opened a tea house at Yiwu in the 13th year of Yongzheng (1735). The name is explained as meaning shared celebration across the land. Tea from before 1910 is treated as the peak.

The dragon-and-horse ticket was used until about 1920. Faced with growing imitation, the owners Liu Shunshu and Liu Kuiguang, father and son, then changed it to the double-lion design.

After 1949 the business went through joint state-private ownership, and family production in Yiwu stopped. In 1994 Taiwanese tea men looking for old pu-erh found the area dormant and recruited two surviving employees of the old factory to make what became the Zhenchun Yahao tea. The present company, based in Jinghong, received the Yunnan time-honoured brand title in 2011.
